description.summary: The kappa (河童, 'river child') is one of the most famous yōkai in Japanese folklore: a child-sized amphibious water-spirit with a turtle-like shell, beaked face, and a water-filled dish (sara) on its head whose drying or spilling renders it powerless.
description.full: The kappa (河童, 'river child'; also kawatarō, kawako, garappa, and at least eighty regional names) is a class of water-yokai in Japanese folklore, prototypically the size of a human child, greenish, with a turtle-like carapace, webbed hands and feet, a beaked face, and a circular depression on the crown of the head — the sara — which holds water. The water in the sara is the kappa's source of supernatural power; if it spills or dries out, the kappa is paralysed or killed, which gives rise to the well-known folk defense of bowing deeply (the polite kappa returns the bow, spilling the dish). Kappa are river- and pond-dwelling, associated with sumo wrestling, with attempts to drag horses, cattle, and people into the water, and with the extraction of the mythical 'shirikodama' (尻子玉) — a small ball of life-essence said to lie inside the human anus. They are notoriously fond of cucumbers (giving the name kappamaki to cucumber sushi rolls). Early systematic descriptions appear in the Edo-period encyclopedia Wakan Sansai Zue (和漢三才図会, 1712) by Terajima Ryōan, and the kappa is depicted in Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776). Folkloric documentation continued under modern researchers, especially Yanagita Kunio (1875–1962), whose Tōno Monogatari (遠野物語, 1910) records numerous kappa accounts from Tōno, Iwate, and Lafcadio Hearn (1850–1904), who wrote on kappa in his collections of Japanese folklore. The kappa remains a beloved figure of Japanese popular culture, appearing on signage, in advertising (notably the Kappa beverage and snack brand), in manga, film (Akira Kurosawa's Dreams (1990) and Hayao Miyazaki's Spirited Away (2001) feature kappa-like figures), and as a regional symbol in towns such as Tōno, Ushiku, and Saga.

etymology.origin: Japanese kappa (河童) = kawa (川, 'river') + warawa / wappa (童, 'child'); regional variants include kawatarō, kawako, and garappa
etymology.first_use: Recorded in Edo-period literature, including Wakan Sansai Zue (1712); folk usage long predates

related_phenomena.name: Suijin
related_phenomena.description: Shinto water-deity; conceptual ancestor of many kappa traditions

related_phenomena.name: Hyōsube
related_phenomena.description: Kyushu variant of the kappa, especially around Saga

related_phenomena.name: Vodyanoy
related_phenomena.description: Slavic male water-spirit; comparable river-dwelling trickster role

features.description: Concave depression on the crown of the head holding water; the source of the kappa's strength. If spilled or dried, the kappa is incapacitated
Hard, often greenish shell on the back
Aquatic adaptations on hands and feet
Slick, scaly green or yellow-green skin

physical.morphology: Bipedal humanoid with reptilian / amphibian features; child-sized stature.

abilities.description: Kappa are famously fond of sumo and challenge humans to wrestling matches
Skilled swimmers; ambush prey from rivers and ponds
Reaches into a victim through the anus to remove the mythical 'shirikodama' (尻子玉), a ball of vital essence
Compulsive politeness: if a human bows, the kappa bows back, spilling the water from its sara and rendering it helpless
In some traditions, severed kappa arms can be reattached

behavior.diet: Cucumbers (preferred offering), fish, and the shirikodama / blood / liver of human victims
patterns: Most active at dusk and at night
Strongly territorial in particular pools and river-bends
Often pacified by offerings of cucumbers (the basis of kappamaki sushi)
Dragging horses, cattle, and children into water is a recurring motif
May sometimes be befriended; occasionally portrayed as helpful

range.description: Found throughout Japanese folklore, with strong regional concentrations in Kyushu (garappa, hyōsube) and Tōhoku (Tōno).

hotspots.name: Tōno (遠野)

location.description: Town and basin in Iwate Prefecture, focus of Yanagita Kunio's foundational folklore collection

hotspots.notes: Site of Yanagita Kunio's Tōno Monogatari (1910); the Kappa-buchi (河童淵) pool is a celebrated folkloric location

hotspots.name: Ushiku (牛久市)
hotspots.notes: Historically associated with kappa lore; modern Ushiku-numa marsh and city signage feature kappa motifs

hotspots.name: Saga Prefecture
hotspots.notes: Stronghold of garappa / hyōsube regional variants

peak_activity_periods.description: Codification of kappa lore in encyclopedias, kaidan, and Sekien's bestiary
Modern folkloric documentation (Yanagita's Tōno Monogatari) and pop-culture entrenchment

origins.cultural_roots: Shinto water-deity (suijin) tradition syncretized with Buddhist and continental Asian water-spirit motifs (notably the Chinese suiko 'water tiger').
origins.earliest_accounts: Terajima Ryōan's Wakan Sansai Zue (1712) is among the earliest systematic descriptions; folk tradition is much older.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to broader East Asian water-yokai (suiko, hyōsube, garappa), to Shinto suijin cults, and to the global pattern of river-dwelling trickster spirits.

timeline.event: Terajima Ryōan publishes the encyclopedia Wakan Sansai Zue (和漢三才図会), with a systematic kappa entry
Toriyama Sekien depicts the kappa in Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (画図百鬼夜行)
Yanagita Kunio publishes Tōno Monogatari (遠野物語), recording numerous kappa stories from Tōno, Iwate
timeline.significance: Foundational text of modern Japanese folklore studies and kappa documentation

history.modern_era: The kappa is one of the most recognizable Japanese cultural icons: present on town mascots, in countless manga and anime, in Hayao Miyazaki's and Hayao Kawai's references, and in commercial branding such as the Kappa snack brand (Calbee, since 1964). Tōno's annual Kappa-related tourism and the Kappa Sushi restaurant chain (since 1979) further entrench the figure.

documentary.name: Wakan Sansai Zue (和漢三才図会)
documentary.description: Edo-period illustrated encyclopedia by Terajima Ryōan with a systematic entry on the kappa.

documentary.name: Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (画図百鬼夜行)
documentary.description: Toriyama Sekien's illustrated yokai compendium, depicting the kappa.

documentary.name: Tōno Monogatari (遠野物語)
documentary.description: Yanagita Kunio's foundational modern folklore collection from Tōno, Iwate, including numerous kappa accounts.

paranormal.name: Shinto water-spirit (suijin) tradition
paranormal.description: The kappa is the popular-folkloric form of older Shinto suijin (water-deity) figures, demoted from formal divinity to trickster yokai over time.

scientific.name: Drowning-cautionary archetype
scientific.description: Kappa lore plausibly functioned (and continues to function) as a parental warning against playing in dangerous river-pools; the shirikodama-extraction motif is a vivid pedagogical image of drowning.
evidence_cited: Concentration of kappa stories around dangerous river bends
Continued use of kappa imagery on Japanese drowning-warning signs

scientific.name: Misidentification of giant salamanders / soft-shelled turtles
scientific.description: Some scholars and naturalists have suggested that early kappa reports may reflect encounters with the Japanese giant salamander (Andrias japonicus) or large soft-shelled turtles in remote rivers.
evidence_cited: Range of A. japonicus overlapping with kappa-rich folklore regions

skeptical.name: Cultural-folkloric figure
skeptical.description: Mainstream understanding treats the kappa as a folkloric and literary figure with no need for cryptozoological commitment; the figure is studied as part of Japanese cultural and religious history.

stories: Tales of kappa drowning horses and children
Tales of kappa befriending humans after being defeated
folklore.beliefs: Modern Japanese culture treats the kappa as folklore rather than living belief, while integrating it deeply into regional identity, signage, and commercial branding.

literature: Lafcadio Hearn — Japanese folklore essays (late 19th century)
Shigeru Mizuki — yokai encyclopedias and 'Kappa no Sanpei' (河童の三平)
Michael Dylan Foster — The Book of Yōkai (2015)
film_tv: Hayao Miyazaki — Spirited Away (2001) — kappa-adjacent river-spirit characters
Summer Days with Coo (河童のクゥと夏休み, 2007, dir. Keiichi Hara)

other: Kappa drowning-warning road signage in Japan
